entities.name: Jan Očko of Vlašim
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jan Očko of Vlašim (1292–1380) ascended to become the second Archbishop of Prague (1364–1378) and the first Bohemian cardinal, marking a pinnacle of ecclesiastical power within the Kingdom of Bohemia during the zenith of Emperor Charles IV's reign. His remarkable career, spanning nearly seven decades, was deeply intertwined with the Luxembourg dynasty's strategic efforts to consolidate both spiritual and temporal authority in Central Europe, ultimately elevating Prague to a major European religious and cultural center. As a trusted confidant and principal advisor to Charles IV, Očko played a crucial, often understated, role in shaping the imperial court's diplomatic and ecclesiastical policies, particularly in relations with the Holy See.

Prior to his archiepiscopal appointment, Očko demonstrated significant administrative acumen as Bishop of Olomouc (1351–1364) and concurrently as Chancellor of the Kingdom of Bohemia. His elevation to the Archbishopric of Prague in 1364, succeeding the pioneering Arnošt of Pardubice, saw him continue the vital work of establishing the archdiocese's independence and prestige within the Holy Roman Empire. A crowning achievement came in 1378, when Pope Urban VI elevated him to the College of Cardinals, bestowing the rare distinction of Cardinal-Priest of Santi XII Apostoli, a testament to his personal influence and the considerable political leverage of Charles IV. He was also instrumental in securing the election of Charles's son, Wenceslaus IV, as King of the Romans in 1376, further solidifying the Luxembourg succession.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jan Očko's tenure as Archbishop of Prague and his elevation to cardinal marked a peak for Bohemian ecclesiastical power, directly influencing the political and cultural landscape of Central Europe under Charles IV. His career solidified Prague's role as a major spiritual capital and set precedents for future Bohemian church leaders.
